tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If you heat ice, it melts.
If the library opens early, Maya will finish her essay before lunch.
If it rains tomorrow, we will cancels the picnic.
If Leo studies tonight, he passes the quiz for certain next week.
If the oven is ready, Sara will bakes the muffins.
tactical_explanations:
**A) If you heat ice, it melts.**

This is a clean zero conditional: a general scientific fact uses present simple on both sides. Heating ice always leads to melting, so there is no need for will. The sentence reads like a law of nature, which is exactly when zero is the right frame.

Present simple on both sides is exactly how zero conditional marks a timeless physical law, so the ice-melting wording is true.
**B) If the library opens early, Maya will finish her essay before lunch.**

A real morning plan: present simple after if, will + base verb in the result. Opening early is possible, and finishing before lunch is an open future outcome. That present-plus-will pairing is the classic first conditional.

A real morning schedule wants present after if and will in the result, so the library-and-essay line is true.
**C) If it rains tomorrow, we will cancels the picnic.**

After will the verb must stay bare — "will cancels" → "will cancel". The if-clause is fine (present for a real future); only the result form is broken. Modals never take a third-person -s on the following verb.

**Trap:** will cancels looks almost like ordinary present, but will freezes the next verb as V1.

Will freezes the next verb as a bare infinitive, so will cancels is false — "If it rains tomorrow, we will cancel the picnic."
**D) If Leo studies tonight, he passes the quiz for certain next week.**

A real future result pinned to next week needs will pass (or similar), not bare present passes. Present + present would only fit a zero-style habit or general truth. This next-week quiz is an open plan, not a law of nature.

**Trap:** bare present in the result can look tidy, but next week forces a will result.

Next week is an open future result, not a zero-conditional habit, so bare passes is false: "If Leo studies tonight, he will pass the quiz for certain next week."
**E) If the oven is ready, Sara will bakes the muffins.**

Will takes the base form bake, not bakes. The condition is a fine first-conditional if-clause; only the -s after will wrecks the result. Strip the inflection and the open-future plan is clean.

The -s after will breaks the modal pattern, so the muffin line is false — "If the oven is ready, Sara will bake the muffins."
tasks.solution_overview:
Ice, library hours, rain, study night, and muffins — a starter round on zero versus first conditionals.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Zero conditionals state general facts with present simple in both clauses (heat ice → it melts). First conditionals state open, real futures: present after if, will + base verb in the result. The broken lines either glue an -s onto the verb after will, or use bare present where a next-week future result needs will.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask: always true, or a real plan? Facts stay present + present. Real plans keep present in the if-clause and will + V1 in the result. If you see will cancels / will bakes, strip the -s. If the result is pinned to next week and the condition is real, prefer will pass over passes.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If plants get no water, they die.
If Nora books the tickets today, we will sit together on the train.
If the bus is late, Tom will misses his lecture.
If you mix red and blue, you will get purple every time as a law of nature.
If the gym opens at six, Ana will train before work.
tactical_explanations:
**A) If plants get no water, they die.**

Zero conditional correctly states a general consequence with present simple on both sides. No water → death is a habitual natural truth, not a one-off future plan. Will would wrongly pull this permanent result into a first-conditional frame.

Habitual natural consequence belongs in present + present, so the no-water wording stands as zero conditional.
**B) If Nora books the tickets today, we will sit together on the train.**

First conditional links a real booking decision today to a future seating plan. Present in the if-clause, will + base verb in the result — textbook open future. Both halves stay aligned with a possible today → later chain.

Today’s booking and later seating form a clean open-future chain, so present + will sit is the right frame.
**C) If the bus is late, Tom will misses his lecture.**

Will misses is ungrammatical; use "will miss". The late-bus condition is fine first-conditional material — only the -s after will is wrong. Keep the verb after will in the bare infinitive.

**Trap:** will misses mirrors third-person present, so it looks almost right at speed.

Third-person -s has no place after will, so will misses is false: "If the bus is late, Tom will miss his lecture."
**D) If you mix red and blue, you will get purple every time as a law of nature.**

A timeless colour fact belongs in zero conditional (you get purple), not first with will. The phrase as a law of nature is a strong clue that will is the wrong mood for a permanent truth. Drop will and keep both clauses in present simple.

**Trap:** will get feels natural for results, but a named law of nature wants zero, not first.

A named law of nature needs zero, not will in the result, so the colour line is false — "If you mix red and blue, you get purple every time as a law of nature."
**E) If the gym opens at six, Ana will train before work.**

Clean first conditional for a real morning timetable and intention. Opens is present; will train is the open future result. Nothing in the line forces a zero-style habit frame.

Opens for a real early opening plus will train for intention is classic first conditional, so Ana’s gym plan is true.
tasks.solution_overview:
Plants, train seats, a late bus, mixing colours, and an early gym — more zero-versus-first practice, including a fact wrongly dressed in will.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Always-true consequences belong in zero (present + present). Open plans belong in first (present + will). One line fails with will + -s; another states a permanent colour law with will get, which pulls a timeless fact into first conditional.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Label each sentence fact or plan. Facts: drop will and keep both presents. Plans: keep will + bare verb. Reject will misses on sight, and reject will when the result is framed as a law of nature.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If I were you, I would take the earlier train.
If the weather were better, we would cycle to the lake.
If she would have more free time, she would join the choir.
If Dan lived closer, he would walk to campus every day.
If I was the team captain tomorrow in this hypothetical, I would change the formation.
tactical_explanations:
**A) If I were you, I would take the earlier train.**

Second conditional with formal were after if I, plus would + base verb for unreal advice. The speaker is not claiming to be you — the role is hypothetical. This is the classic advice pattern exams reward.

Unreal advice after if I takes were + would, so the earlier-train suggestion is true.
**B) If the weather were better, we would cycle to the lake.**

Past/were in the if-clause plus would marks an unreal present wish about the weather. We are not claiming the weather is better — we are imagining it. Would cycle is the unreal result that depends on that imagined improvement.

Imagined better weather with were and would cycle is textbook unreal present, so the lake line is true.
**C) If she would have more free time, she would join the choir.**

Do not put would in the if-clause; write "If she had more free time, she would join the choir." Keep would for the result only; the condition wants past simple. Stacking would on both sides is a classic second-conditional break.

**Trap:** If she would have … looks polite, but standard conditionals ban would in the if-clause.

Would belongs only in the result, so stacking it in the if-clause is false — "If she had more free time, she would join the choir."
**D) If Dan lived closer, he would walk to campus every day.**

Standard second conditional for a counterfactual present about distance and commuting. Lived + would walk is the default unreal-present frame. Dan does not live closer; the daily walk is only imagined.

Lived closer is counterfactual present with would walk as the imagined commute, so Dan’s line is true.
**E) If I was the team captain tomorrow in this hypothetical, I would change the formation.**

Careful exam English prefers were for unreal be after if, not was, especially in formal true/false items. The rest of the pattern (would change) is fine; only was is the fail. Swap "was" → "were" and the hypothetical captain role is exam-safe.

**Trap:** If I was is common in speech, so it can feel acceptable — exams still prefer were here.

Formal exam English wants were for unreal be after if, so was is false: "If I were the team captain tomorrow in this hypothetical, I would change the formation."
tasks.solution_overview:
Trains, weather, choir, campus walks, and team captain — unreal present (second conditional) with exam-style were and a would-in-the-if trap.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Second conditional marks unreal or hypothetical present/future: past simple or were in the if-clause, would + base verb in the result. Do not park would inside the if-clause. Careful exam English prefers were over was for unreal be after if.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check where would sits — result only. Prefer If I were / If the weather were for hypothetical be. Keep past simple + would for counterfactual present lifestyle wishes (distance, commuting).

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Unless it rains, the match will go ahead.
As long as you water the herbs, they will stay fresh.
Unless you will hurry, we will miss the opening credits.
If only I knew her phone number now.
I wish I can speak Italian fluently this semester.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Unless it rains, the match will go ahead.**

Unless (= if not) + present simple pairs cleanly with will for a real future sports plan. The match goes ahead if rain does not intervene. Will sits in the result, not in the unless-clause.

Unless already packs if not, and present + will maps a real sports plan, so the match-ahead wording is true.
**B) As long as you water the herbs, they will stay fresh.**

As long as (= provided that) takes present simple for a real ongoing condition, then will in the result. Watering is the proviso that keeps the herbs fine. The connector behaves like if for open conditions.

As long as behaves like if for open provisos, so water + will stay fresh is the right herb frame.
**C) Unless you will hurry, we will miss the opening credits.**

After unless, avoid will; use present — "Unless you hurry, we will miss the opening credits." Will belongs in the result, not stacked into the condition. The double will makes the polarity and timing messy.

**Trap:** Unless you will hurry mirrors ordinary future talk, but unless rarely takes will.

Unless rarely hosts will, so the double-will condition is false — "Unless you hurry, we will miss the opening credits."
**D) If only I knew her phone number now.**

If only + past simple correctly wishes about an unreal present lack of knowledge. Knew is the backshifted form for a present gap. The speaker does not have the number now, so past form carries the regret.

Knew is the right backshift for a present knowledge gap after if only, so the phone-number wish is true.
**E) I wish I can speak Italian fluently this semester.**

Wish about present ability needs past form — "can" → "could" ("I wish I could speak…"). After wish, shift the tense back one step from reality. Ordinary present modal can does not belong after wish.

**Trap:** I wish I can … keeps everyday present can, which looks fluent but fails the backshift.

Wish demands a tense step back, so present can is false: "I wish I could speak Italian fluently this semester."
tasks.solution_overview:
Match day, herbs, film credits, a missing number, and Italian — unless, as long as, and wish / if only at entry level.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Unless and as long as behave like if for real conditions: present in the condition clause, will (or another realistic result) in the main clause. Wish and if only for present unreal situations shift the tense back — past simple, and can becomes could.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Strip will from unless / if / as long as conditions. For present regrets with wish / if only, use past simple. Reject I wish I can… on sight.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the cinema had more evening slots, we would go more often.
If I had known about the sale, I would have bought the jacket.
If they would practise every day, they would improve faster.
Unless Mia finishes her lab report, she will not watch the film.
As long as the neighbours keep quiet, I can revise until midnight.
tactical_explanations:
**A) If the cinema had more evening slots, we would go more often.**

Second conditional for an unreal present about the cinema timetable. Had (past meaning) + would go imagines a better schedule that does not actually exist. The go-more-often result depends on that counterfactual slots claim.

Past-form had plus would go imagines slots that don’t exist, so the cinema wish stands as second conditional.
**B) If I had known about the sale, I would have bought the jacket.**

Third conditional: past perfect in the if-clause and would have + past participle for a missed past opportunity. The sale is over; the jacket stays unbought in this alternate past. Both halves stay locked in closed unreal past.

Closed sale, closed jacket opportunity: past perfect and would have bought lock both halves in unreal past, so the line is true.
**C) If they would practise every day, they would improve faster.**

Would does not belong in the if-clause; use "If they practised every day, they would improve faster." Ban would from the condition; leave it for the result. Double would is the signature second-conditional error here.

**Trap:** If they would practise … can sound like polite pressure, but the if-clause wants past simple.

Double would in the if-clause breaks second conditional, so the practise line is false — "If they practised every day, they would improve faster."
**D) Unless Mia finishes her lab report, she will not watch the film.**

Unless + present correctly sets a real study condition before a future entertainment plan. Finishes is present; will not watch is the open future result. Unless already means if not, so one layer of negation is enough.

Unless + present before will not watch cleanly gates Mia’s film plan, so the study proviso is true.
**E) As long as the neighbours keep quiet, I can revise until midnight.**

As long as + present states a real proviso that enables present ability with can. Not every as long as line needs will — can / may work when the result is present capability. Keep quiet stays present; can revise is the enabled present result.

A present capability result with can sits fine under as long as + present, so the midnight revision frame is true.
tasks.solution_overview:
Cinema slots, a missed sale, daily practice, a lab report, and quiet neighbours — blending second, third, unless, and as long as.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Second conditional = unreal present (past + would). Third = unreal past (had + V3 / would have + V3). Unless and as long as keep present for real provisos. The clear fail is would parked inside the if-clause.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Locate would: only the result may have it in these patterns. Match unreal-present cinema wishes to past + would, and missed past shopping to past perfect + would have. Trust unless / as long as when the condition stays present.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the ferry had left on time, we would have reached the island before dusk.
Had she set an alarm, she would not have overslept.
If Ben had trained harder, he will have won the race.
I wish I had packed an umbrella yesterday.
If only the Wi-Fi worked in this café right now.
tactical_explanations:
**A) If the ferry had left on time, we would have reached the island before dusk.**

Classic third conditional for a missed travel outcome in the past. Had left + would have reached keeps both halves in unreal past. The ferry did not leave on time, and the island arrival before dusk did not happen.

Had left and would have reached are the matching unreal-past halves, so the missed ferry outcome is true.
**B) Had she set an alarm, she would not have overslept.**

Inverted third conditional (Had she set…) correctly replaces If she had set… The meaning and the would not have overslept result stay fully unreal past. Inversion is a formal shortcut, not a different tense.

Had she set… is only an inverted if she had set…, so the overslept alternate past is true.
**C) If Ben had trained harder, he will have won the race.**

The result must stay in the unreal past — "will have won" → "would have won". Will have is ordinary future perfect, not third-conditional regret. Past perfect in the if-clause forces would have in the result.

**Trap:** will have won looks like a polished perfect form, but third conditional needs would have.

Third conditional needs would have, not future-perfect will have, so Ben’s race line is false — "If Ben had trained harder, he would have won the race."
**D) I wish I had packed an umbrella yesterday.**

Wish + past perfect correctly regrets a past packing choice. Yesterday locks the regret in closed past, so past perfect is the right shift. A present wish would use past simple instead.

Yesterday forces a past perfect after wish, so the umbrella regret is true.
**E) If only the Wi-Fi worked in this café right now.**

If only + past simple correctly wishes about an unreal present problem. Right now signals present inconvenience, so worked (past form) is the backshift — not past perfect. Past perfect would wrongly push the café Wi-Fi problem into finished past.

Right now keeps the café problem in present, so if only + past simple worked is the fitting wish.
tasks.solution_overview:
Ferry timing, a missed alarm, a race, an umbrella, and café Wi-Fi — unreal past with third conditional, Had-inversion, and wish / if only.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Unreal past uses had + V3 in the condition and would have + V3 in the result. Had she set… is a formal inversion of If she had set… Wish / if only take past perfect for closed past regrets and past simple for present inconvenience. Reject will have where would have is required.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Ask whether the regret is finished (past perfect / would have) or present (past simple after if only). Accept inversion as a shortcut for if + past perfect. Swap will have won → would have won in third-conditional results.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If you don't water the tomatoes, they will wilt.
Unless you don't water the tomatoes, they will wilt.
As long as students submit drafts on Friday, the tutor will give feedback on Monday.
I wish the neighbours would stop drilling at dawn.
If only she will listen to the podcast before the seminar.
tactical_explanations:
**A) If you don't water the tomatoes, they will wilt.**

First conditional with a negative if-clause correctly predicts a real future result. Don't water is still present tense after if; will wilt is the open outcome. Negation in the condition does not force a different conditional type.

Negation in the if-clause doesn’t change type: present + will still predicts the open wilt, so the tomato line is true.
**B) Unless you don't water the tomatoes, they will wilt.**

Unless already means if not, so Unless you don't creates a messy double negative. Use "Unless you water…" or "If you don't…" — not both layers of negation. The intended polarity becomes unclear, and exam English rejects the stack.

**Trap:** Unless you don't … can look carefully cautious, but the double negation is the fail.

Unless already means if not, so stacking don’t creates muddy polarity: "Unless you water the tomatoes, they will wilt."
**C) As long as students submit drafts on Friday, the tutor will give feedback on Monday.**

As long as + present correctly sets a real academic condition for a future result. Submit is present; will give is the open Monday plan. Provided / as long as behave like if for real conditions.

Friday drafts as present proviso and Monday feedback with will is open academic planning, so the as-long-as frame is true.
**D) I wish the neighbours would stop drilling at dawn.**

Wish + would correctly complains about someone else's annoying present habit and asks for a change. This is the behaviour-change use of wish, not a simple state wish. Would stop is the plea for different neighbour behaviour.

Wish + would is the behaviour-change plea, so the dawn-drilling complaint is true.
**E) If only she will listen to the podcast before the seminar.**

If only for a present/future wish needs past or would, not will — "If only she would listen…" / "If only she listened…". Ordinary will does not belong after if only. Keep will for ordinary first-conditional results, not wishful if only clauses.

**Trap:** If only she will … feels like urgent future hopes, but if only rejects ordinary will.

If only rejects ordinary will, so the podcast hope is false — "If only she would listen to the podcast before the seminar."
tasks.solution_overview:
Tomatoes, drafts, dawn drilling, and a podcast — polarity with unless, as long as for real plans, and wish / if only + would for behaviour change.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

If + negative present + will is fine for open futures. Unless already means if not, so Unless you don't creates a messy double negative. Wish + would complains about someone else's habit; if only for a present/future wish needs past or would, not ordinary will.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Avoid stacking unless with another negative. Keep as long as in present for real academic plans. Prefer wish / if only + would (or past) when you want a change in behaviour — reject if only … will.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If the trail were less muddy, we would hike further.
If prices fall next month, more families will switch to seasonal produce.
If I would be taller, I would reach the top shelf easily.
Unless the museum closes early, we will see the sculpture wing.
I wish I were better at mental arithmetic.
tactical_explanations:
**A) If the trail were less muddy, we would hike further.**

Second conditional with were for an unreal present outdoor scenario. The trail is muddy; we only imagine it cleaner. Would hike is the unreal result that depends on that cleaner trail.

Muddy trail now, cleaner trail only imagined: were + would hike is the right unreal pair, so the wording is true.
**B) If prices fall next month, more families will switch to seasonal produce.**

First conditional: a real possible price change pairs with will switch. Fall is present; will switch is the open future lifestyle result. Nothing here is hypothetical enough to force second conditional.

A possible next-month price drop pairs with will switch, so present + will correctly frames the produce shift.
**C) If I would be taller, I would reach the top shelf easily.**

Never write "If I would be"; use "If I were" / "If I was" (exam: were). Would stays out of the if-clause in standard conditionals; only the result may keep would reach. The height wish is unreal present, so were is the safe condition form.

**Trap:** If I would be … doubles would and looks like cautious future English — it is still wrong.

Would never opens the if-clause for height wishes, so If I would be is false: "If I were taller, I would reach the top shelf easily."
**D) Unless the museum closes early, we will see the sculpture wing.**

Unless + present + will correctly frames a real museum visit plan. Closes is present; will see is the open result if early closing does not intervene. Unless already means if not, so the polarity is clear.

Unless + present + will keeps the museum visit open unless early closing intervenes, so the sculpture plan is true.
**E) I wish I were better at mental arithmetic.**

Wish + were correctly marks an unreal present ability. Formal exam English likes were here for present counterfactuals with be. The speaker is not better at mental arithmetic now — were carries that gap.

Wish + were marks an unreal present skill gap, so the mental-arithmetic line is true.
tasks.solution_overview:
Muddy trails, seasonal produce, shelf height, a museum wing, and mental arithmetic — consolidating second conditional, unless, wish + were, and one real first-conditional line.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Unreal present keeps were / past + would. Real futures keep present + will. Unless + present + will frames real visit plans. The signature trap is If I would be… — would must not sit in the if-clause.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept were for unreal outdoor and ability wishes. Accept one clean first-conditional price/lifestyle line. Rewrite If I would be → If I were. Trust unless when the condition stays present.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If she had taken the earlier bus, she would be at the theatre now.
If he were more organised, he would have handed in the portfolio last Friday.
If they had left earlier, they would arrive yesterday evening.
If I had more patience as a child, I would have learned piano sooner.
If you heated the soup now, it would taste better.
tactical_explanations:
**A) If she had taken the earlier bus, she would be at the theatre now.**

Mixed conditional: past unreal cause (had taken) with present result (would be). The missed bus is finished; the empty seat at the theatre is the present consequence. Matching cause time to result time is what makes the mix legal.

**Tip:** Past perfect in if + would + V1 → past cause, present effect.

Past-perfect cause and present would-be result each own their time, so the bus → theatre mix is true.
**B) If he were more organised, he would have handed in the portfolio last Friday.**

Mixed conditional: unreal present character (were) with past result (would have handed). The trait is imagined as present; the missed Friday deadline is the past fallout. Were keeps the personality claim unreal now; would have locks the Friday fail in the past.

**Tip:** If + past / were + would have + V3 → present unreal trait, past consequence.

Present unreal were feeding would have handed on Friday is a legal present-trait → past-result mix, so the portfolio line is true.
**C) If they had left earlier, they would arrive yesterday evening.**

A finished past result needs would have arrived, not would arrive, after a past perfect condition. Yesterday evening locks the outcome in the past, so plain would + V1 is the wrong half of the mix. Past condition plus past result wants full third conditional.

**Trap:** would arrive can look like a sleek mix, but yesterday evening forces would have arrived.

Yesterday evening locks a past arrival, so plain would arrive is false — "If they had left earlier, they would have arrived yesterday evening."
**D) If I had more patience as a child, I would have learned piano sooner.**

A childhood past state needs past perfect — "If I had had more patience as a child…". Pure past regrets need had + past participle in the if-clause when the cause itself is past. Bare had + noun underpowers the childhood timeline here.

**Trap:** If I had more patience as a child looks almost second-conditional, but as a child pushes it into past.

A childhood cause needs past perfect had had, so bare had underpowers the piano regret: "If I had had more patience as a child, I would have learned piano sooner."
**E) If you heated the soup now, it would taste better.**

Second conditional can use past simple heated for an unreal or unlikely present suggestion. Now softens into a hypothetical offer rather than a firm first-conditional plan. Would taste is the imagined better result under that soft suggestion.

Past heated with would taste softens a present soup offer into second conditional, so the wording is true.
highlights: If I had more patience as a child
tasks.solution_overview:
Theatre arrival, a late portfolio, yesterday's arrival, childhood patience, and soup — mixed conditionals and time alignment.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Mixed conditionals match the time of the cause to the time of the result: past perfect cause + present would result, or unreal present trait + would have past result. Reject would + V1 with clear past time markers like yesterday, and reject weak past-perfect gaps when the story is a childhood past state.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Underline time cues (now, last Friday, yesterday, as a child). Build the if-clause for the cause's time and the result for the effect's time. Soft hypothetical now can still use second conditional (heated / would taste).

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: As long as you will follow the recipe, the cake will rise.
Provided that the pool is open, we will swim after class.
I wish I didn't have to revise tonight.
If only they hadn't cancelled the outdoor concert last Saturday.
Unless she had missed the call, she would answer it now.
tactical_explanations:
**A) As long as you will follow the recipe, the cake will rise.**

As long as takes present for real conditions — "As long as you follow…", not "will follow". Will belongs in the result (will rise), not twice. The double will breaks the open-condition connector pattern.

**Trap:** as long as you will follow feels like careful future English, but the proviso wants present.

As long as wants present in the proviso, so will follow is false — "As long as you follow the recipe, the cake will rise."
**B) Provided that the pool is open, we will swim after class.**

Provided that + present + will is a clean real-future proviso. Is open sets the condition; will swim is the plan. Provided that ≈ if / as long as for open conditions.

Provided that + present + will is the open swim proviso, so the pool line is true.
**C) I wish I didn't have to revise tonight.**

Wish + past simple correctly regrets a present obligation. Didn't have to is the backshift from present have to. Tonight keeps the annoyance in present time, so past simple — not past perfect — is enough.

Tonight’s have-to annoyance only needs past simple after wish, so didn’t have to is the sound backshift.
**D) If only they hadn't cancelled the outdoor concert last Saturday.**

If only + past perfect correctly regrets a finished past cancellation. Last Saturday closes the event in the past. Present-backshift past simple would underpower that closed-date regret.

Last Saturday closes the concert in finished past, so if only + past perfect correctly carries the regret.
**E) Unless she had missed the call, she would answer it now.**

The timelines clash. A past-perfect unless-clause wants a past result (would have answered), or rephrase carefully as a matching mixed / first pattern. Do not paste past perfect onto plain would + V1 present without a clear mixed design.

**Trap:** Unless she had missed… would answer now looks mixed at a glance, but the times do not lock cleanly.

Past-perfect unless and plain would answer now don’t lock, so the call line is false — "Unless she had missed the call, she would have answered it."
tasks.solution_overview:
Cake rising, a swim plan, revision, a cancelled concert, and a missed call — connectors plus wish / if only tense shifts, with one messy unless timeline.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

As long as / provided that take present for real conditions, not will. Wish + past simple regrets present obligations; if only + past perfect regrets finished past cancellations. Unless + past perfect wants a time-matched result — not a casually pasted present would + V1 without a clear mixed pattern.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Keep will out of as long as / provided that. Trust didn't / hadn't after wish / if only when the time cue is clear. For unless + had missed, either go fully past (would have answered) or rebuild a clean mixed / first pattern — do not leave the clash.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 11
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.

tactical_explanations:
**A) If the tutor explained the theorem more slowly, more students would have passed last week's test.**

Mixed conditional: unreal present teaching style (explained) with a finished past result (would have passed). The slow-explanation habit is imagined as a present trait; last week's scores are the past consequence. Cause time and result time each get the form that matches them.

**Tip:** If + past + would have + V3 → present unreal trait, past consequence.

Explained as a present teaching trait with would have passed last week is a legal mix, so the tutor line is true.
**B) If the tutor had explained the theorem more slowly, more students would pass the resit next month.**

A finished past explanation (had explained) does not pair cleanly with plain future would pass next month. Use would have passed for a past test, or If she explained… would pass for unreal present/future. The times of cause and result must align before the line can pass.

**Trap:** had explained + would pass next month mixes closed past with open future without a legal hinge.

Closed-past had explained cannot feed open-future would pass next month, so the times fail — rebuild as "would have passed" for a past test, or "explained" / "would pass" for unreal now.
**C) If the tutor had explained the theorem more slowly last term, more students would understand it now.**

Mixed: past unreal teaching (had explained) with present result (would understand now). Last term is the cause; now is the effect. Past perfect in the if-clause and would + V1 in the result is the standard past→present mix.

Last-term past perfect cause and would understand now match past→present, so the theorem mix is true.
**D) Had the trail been clearer, we would not have got lost.**

Inverted third conditional correctly reports a past hiking mishap avoided in an alternate past. Had the trail been… replaces If the trail had been… Would not have got lost keeps the result in unreal past.

Had the trail been… simply inverts if + past perfect, so the lost-on-the-trail alternate past is true.
**E) If it weren't for the fog, we could see the harbour lights.**

If it weren't for + noun correctly introduces an unreal present obstacle, with could in the result. Without the fog, the lights would be visible now. Weren't for marks the fog as the present barrier.

Weren’t for names fog as the present barrier with could see as the blocked result, so the harbour line is true.
tasks.solution_overview:
Tutor explanations, a hiking trail, and harbour fog — mixed timelines, Had-inversion, and If it weren't for.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Mixed lines succeed when cause time and result time match (present unreal teaching + past test result; past unreal teaching + present understanding). A finished past explanation (had explained) does not pair cleanly with a plain would pass next month. Inversion and If it weren't for are standard alternate forms.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Check last week's test versus next month's resit versus now. Accept Had the trail been… as third-conditional inversion. Accept If it weren't for + noun for an unreal present obstacle with could / would.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 12
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I wish you wouldn't leave your shoes in the hallway.
I wish you don't leave your shoes in the hallway.
If only the semester break were longer.
If water freezes, it will expands.
If water freezes, it expands.
tactical_explanations:
**A) I wish you wouldn't leave your shoes in the hallway.**

Wish + would correctly asks for a change in habitual annoying behaviour. The shoes keep appearing; wouldn't leave is the plea to stop. This behaviour-change use is distinct from a simple state wish.

Wish + would targets recurring hallway behaviour, so the shoe plea is true.
**B) I wish you don't leave your shoes in the hallway.**

Wish does not take present simple like a command; use wouldn't leave or didn't leave. After wish, shift the tense — don't keep ordinary present. The hallway complaint needs a backshift, not a direct present imperative shape.

**Trap:** I wish you don't … sounds like a firm request, but wish still demands the backshift.

Ordinary present after wish skips the required backshift, so don’t leave is false — "I wish you wouldn’t leave your shoes in the hallway."
**C) If only the semester break were longer.**

If only + were correctly wishes for an unreal present length of break. The break is not longer; were marks the counterfactual. Past perfect would wrongly push the semester-break wish into finished past.

Were marks the break length as counterfactual now, so if only + were is true.
**D) If water freezes, it will expands.**

A scientific fact belongs in zero conditional, and will expands is doubly wrong (will + -s). Write "it expands" — present + present, no will. Permanent physical laws do not take first-conditional will.

**Trap:** will expands piles a wrong mood and a wrong -s onto a timeless fact.

A physical law can’t take will expands (wrong mood and wrong -s), so the freeze line is false: "If water freezes, it expands."
**E) If water freezes, it expands.**

Clean zero conditional for a physical law. Both clauses stay in present simple for a permanent truth. Freezing → expanding is always true, so will is unnecessary.

Present + present is the permanent-law shape, so the "freezing" → "expanding" wording is true.
highlights: If only the semester break were
tasks.solution_overview:
Hallway shoes, semester break, and freezing water — wish + would versus illegal wish + present, if only + were, and a return to zero conditional form.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Wish + would asks someone to change a habit; wish does not take ordinary present like a command. If only + were marks present counterfactuals. Scientific facts belong in zero (present + present); will expands is doubly wrong (wrong mood and will + -s).

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Prefer wouldn't / didn't after wish for behaviour and states. Accept were after if only for present unreal length. For physical laws, keep both clauses present and never write will + -s.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 13
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If she studied abroad next year, she would improve her Spanish dramatically.
If she will study abroad next year, she improves her Spanish dramatically.
Should you need extra towels, the reception desk will help.
Were the path safer, children would use it after dark.
Had we known the gallery was free on Mondays, we would visit yesterday.
tactical_explanations:
**A) If she studied abroad next year, she would improve her Spanish dramatically.**

Second conditional can mark an unlikely or tentative future plan (studied / would improve). Next year does not force first conditional when the speaker treats the plan as remote. Past + would softens the abroad year into a hypothetical step.

**Tip:** Unlikely future → past + would, even with a future time cue like next year.

Treating next year as remote licenses past + would, so the abroad hypothesis is true.
**B) If she will study abroad next year, she improves her Spanish dramatically.**

Will in the if-clause plus bare present improves is a broken first-conditional attempt. Real future: "If she studies…" → "she will improve…". Keep will out of the if-clause and put it in the result.

**Trap:** If she will study … she improves flips the will into the wrong clause and drops it from the result.

Will in the if-clause and bare improves in the result flip first conditional, so the line is false — "If she studies abroad next year, she will improve her Spanish dramatically."
**C) Should you need extra towels, the reception desk will help.**

Should you need… is a polite inverted first-conditional alternative to If you need… Formal offers often prefer this shape. Will help keeps the open real result.

Should you need… is polite inversion of if you need, with will help as the open offer, so the towels line is true.
**D) Were the path safer, children would use it after dark.**

Were the path safer… correctly inverts a second-conditional if-clause. It replaces If the path were safer… with the same unreal-present meaning. Would use is the unreal result after dark.

Were the path safer… equates to if the path were safer, so the after-dark unreal result is true.
**E) Had we known the gallery was free on Mondays, we would visit yesterday.**

Inverted past perfect needs would have visited for a past result, not would visit yesterday. Yesterday forces third-conditional result shape. Had we known… only works when the result stays in unreal past.

**Trap:** would visit yesterday looks like a light mix, but yesterday locks the result into would have + V3.

Yesterday forces would have visited after inverted had we known, so would visit is false: "Had we known the gallery was free on Mondays, we would have visited yesterday."
tasks.solution_overview:
Study abroad, hotel towels, a safer path, and a free gallery day — unlikely futures plus Should / Were / Had inversion.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Second conditional can mark an unlikely future (studied / would improve) even with next year. Real futures keep will out of the if-clause. Should you need… and Were the path safer… are polite inverted forms. Had-inversion for past knowledge needs would have + V3 for a yesterday result.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Reject If she will study… she improves…. Accept Should / Were inversion as formal if-alternatives. Pair Had we known… with would have visited for finished past outcomes — not would visit yesterday.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 14
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: If it had not been for the flat tyre, we would be camping by the lake tonight.

tactical_explanations:
**A) If it had not been for the flat tyre, we would be camping by the lake tonight.**

Mixed pattern: past obstacle (had not been) with present/future-facing result (would be camping tonight). The puncture is finished; tonight's campsite is the imagined present. If it had not been for X is the formal past-cause frame for that mix.

**Tip:** If it had not been for X + would + V1 → past cause, present effect.

Had not been for the puncture plus would be camping tonight aligns past cause with present effect, so the mix is true.
**B) But for the flat tyre, we would be camping by the lake tonight.**

But for + noun is a compact equivalent of if it were not / had not been for. Same camping counterfactual, tighter wording. The flat tyre remains the blocking condition for tonight's campsite.

But for compresses the same obstacle without changing the counterfactual, so the camping line is true.
**C) If it was not for the flat tyre, we would have arrived hours ago.**

Prefer "If it hadn't been for…" → "would have arrived…" (past) or "If it weren't for…" → "would be…" (present). Was not for with would have is non-standard for this item. Keep weren't for and hadn't been for distinct by time.

**Trap:** If it was not for … would have arrived mixes present-looking was not for with a past result.

Was not for with would have arrived mismatches the standard frames, so it is false — "If it hadn’t been for the flat tyre, we would have arrived hours ago."
**D) As long as nobody objects, we can move the rehearsal to Thursday.**

As long as + present + can correctly sets a real group condition. Objects is present; can move is present capability under that proviso. As long as supports present modal results as well as will.

Nobody objects in present with can move under that proviso is an open group plan, so the rehearsal wording is true.
**E) Unless anyone will complain, we can move the rehearsal to Thursday.**

Unless + will is wrong; use "Unless anyone complains…". Will does not belong in the unless-clause. Keep the condition in present for this open group plan.

**Trap:** Unless anyone will complain inserts future will where unless wants present.

Unless takes present, not will, so will complain is false: "Unless anyone complains, we can move the rehearsal to Thursday."
highlights: If it had not been for
tasks.solution_overview:
Flat tyre camping plans and a Thursday rehearsal — If it had not been for / But for, weren't for versus hadn't been for, and no will after unless.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

If it had not been for + would + V1 mixes past obstacle with present/future-facing result. But for + noun is a compact equivalent. Keep If it weren't for (present) distinct from If it hadn't been for (past). As long as + present can support can; unless must not take will.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept had not been for / But for when the tyre story lands on tonight. Reject was not for + would have as non-standard here. Strip will from unless anyone will complain.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=TRUE, C=FALSE, D=TRUE, E=FALSE

tasks.title: Task 15
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: I wish I would have more free evenings.

tactical_explanations:
**A) I wish I would have more free evenings.**

Wish + would have is wrong for a present lack; use wish + past simple (had). Wish I would have… is a classic exam error for present wishes about states. Free evenings are a present desire, so had — not would have — is the backshift.

**Trap:** I wish I would have … borrows third-conditional furniture for a present state wish.

Present free-evening desires take past simple after wish, not would have, so the line is false — "I wish I had more free evenings."
**B) I wish I had more free evenings.**

Wish + past simple correctly expresses an unreal present desire about free time. Had is the backshift from present have. The speaker does not have those free evenings now.

Had backshifts present have for an unreal present desire, so the free-evenings wish is true.
**C) If only the train hadn't been delayed, we wouldn't be queueing now.**

If only + past perfect cause with wouldn't be now is a valid mixed regret linking past delay to present queue. The delay is finished; the queue is happening. Past perfect after if only can feed a present would/wouldn't result when times match.

Past-perfect delay feeding wouldn’t be queueing now is a clean past→present regret mix, so if only is true.
**D) If the coach hadn't been delayed, we wouldn't be queueing now.**

Same mixed pattern with ordinary if instead of if only. Past unreal cause → present continuous-looking result with wouldn't + be + -ing. If and if only both allow this past→present mix when the times are clear.

The same past cause and present queue with ordinary if is equally legal, so the coach line is true.
**E) Supposing the café closed early, where would we study?**

Supposing + past simple introduces a second-conditional hypothesis with would in the question. Closed + would we study is the tentative-scenario frame. Supposing / suppose ≈ if for tentative scenarios.

Supposing + past with would in the question frames a tentative café scenario, so the wording is true.
tasks.solution_overview:
Free evenings, delayed coaches, and a café that might close — killing wish I would have, keeping mixed past→present, and welcoming supposing.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Wish I would have… is a classic exam error for present wishes; use wish + past simple (had). If only / if + past perfect can feed a present would/wouldn't be … now result. Supposing + past introduces second-conditional hypotheses with would in the question.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

For present state wishes, choose had over would have. Accept mixed delay→queue lines with if or if only. Treat supposing like if + past for tentative scenarios.

**Answer.** A=FALSE, B=TRUE, C=TRUE, D=TRUE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 16
tasks.context: Decide whether each sentence is grammatically correct as written.
statements: Even if the tickets are expensive, we will still go to the festival.

If need be, we can share taxis after the concert.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Even if the tickets are expensive, we will still go to the festival.**

Even if + present + will correctly means the result holds despite the condition. Expense does not block the festival plan. Even if is not ordinary if — the main clause still uses real-future will here.

Even if + present lets will still go hold despite expense, so the festival plan is true.
**B) Even if the tickets were free, we will still stay home.**

Even if + past (were) wants would stay, not will stay. Match even if tense to the result: past → would; present → will. Were free clashes with will stay and breaks the unreal/real pairing.

**Trap:** Even if the tickets were free, we will still… mixes second-conditional were with first-conditional will.

Were free wants would stay, not will stay, so the tense clash is false — "Even if the tickets were free, we would still stay home."
**C) Whether or not it rains, the charity run will start at nine.**

Whether or not + present + will correctly says the run happens regardless of rain. The start time is fixed either way. Whether or not = no matter if.

Whether or not + present + will ignores the rain alternative entirely, so the nine-o’clock start is true.
**D) If so be the weather improves, we will hike.**

If so be is archaic and not exam-standard; use "If the weather improves…". Stick to standard if + present for real futures. Modern keys do not reward this set-phrase fossil.

If so be is archaic fossil, not exam if + present, so the hike line is false: "If the weather improves, we will hike."
**E) If need be, we can share taxis after the concert.**

If need be is an accepted fixed phrase meaning if it is necessary, here with can. Do not "correct" it to if needs be in formal keys. The idiom stands as a set form for this open contingency.

**Tip:** If need be is a set idiom — leave the wording alone.

If need be is the set idiom for if it is necessary, so the taxi contingency is true.
highlights: Even if the tickets were, we will
tasks.solution_overview:
Festival tickets, a charity run, weather, and taxis — even if, whether or not, and fixed if need be, while rejecting tense clashes and archaic if so be.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

Even if + present + will means the result holds despite the condition; even if + past wants would, not will. Whether or not + present + will says the plan happens regardless. If so be is archaic; if need be is an accepted idiom.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Match even if tense to the result mood. Accept whether or not for rain-proof plans. Prefer standard If the weather improves… over if so be, and leave if need be alone as a set phrase.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

tasks.title: Task 17

tactical_explanations:
**A) If she were to apply for the scholarship, she would need two references.**

If she were to apply is a formal second-conditional way to mark a hypothetical future step. Were to + V1 softens the plan into something remote or tentative. Would need keeps the unreal/formal result about references.

**Tip:** If + were to + V1 ≈ unlikely/formal if + past.

Were to + apply softens a remote scholarship step with would need as the formal result, so the wording is true.
**B) If she was to have applied last term, she would need two references now.**

Was to have applied mixed with would need now is over-stacked and non-standard for this item. Prefer clear mixed or third forms; avoid was to have + mismatched results. Formal keys stay on clear were to / had + V3 patterns.

**Trap:** was to have applied + would need now piles formal layers without a clean time match.

Was to have applied stacked against would need now never locks cleanly, so the line is false — rebuild with clear "were to" or "had" + V3 and a matching result time.
**C) Were he to practise daily, his serve would improve within weeks.**

Were he to practise… correctly inverts were to for a hypothetical training plan. Same meaning as If he were to practise… Would improve stays the remote/formal result within weeks.

Were he to practise… inverts if he were to practise, so the serve improvement hypothesis is true.
**D) If I knew then what I know now, I would have chosen a different module.**

Knew then is underpowered for a clear past knowledge gap; the standard line uses had known then. Past counterfactual knowledge → past perfect in the if-clause. Would have chosen already locks the module decision in the past, so the if-clause must match.

**Trap:** If I knew then … looks idiomatic, but then + past ignorance wants had known.

Then-past ignorance needs had known, so bare knew underpowers the hindsight: "If I had known then what I know now, I would have chosen a different module."
**E) If I had known then what I know now, I would have chosen a different module.**

Classic form: past perfect for past ignorance, would have chosen for the past decision. This is the polished exam hindsight pattern. Then and the closed module choice stay fully aligned in unreal past.

Had known then and would have chosen keep cause and decision in unreal past, so the polished hindsight form is true.
tasks.solution_overview:
Scholarships, serving practice, and module choices — advanced were to / Were … to inversion and the polished had known then pattern.

**Part 1: What to watch for.**

If she were to apply is a formal second-conditional hypothetical. Were he to practise… inverts the same idea. Was to have applied stacked with a mismatched result is overcomplicated. Past counterfactual knowledge wants had known then, not underpowered knew then.

**Part 2: How to decide.**

Accept were to / Were … to for formal unlikely steps. Prefer clear mixed or third forms over was to have stacks. Choose If I had known then… would have chosen… for hindsight module regrets.

**Answer.** A=TRUE, B=FALSE, C=TRUE, D=FALSE, E=TRUE

Loud videos, airport departures, and free concert tickets — extending conditional logic into I'd rather you, it's time + past, and suppose.

I'd rather you + past softens a present preference about someone else's behaviour. It's time + past marks present urgency in careful exam English. Suppose + past + would frames a second-conditional daydream. These share the same backshift instinct as wish and second conditionals.

**A) If the inflation rate drops, household budgets will feel less pressure next quarter.**

**B) Had the storm not hit, the outdoor market would still be open this afternoon.**

Had the storm not hit feeding would still be open this afternoon is a legal past→present mix, so the market wording is true.
**C) If only I could have attended the reunion last month.**

**D) I wish I could have attended the reunion last month.**

Accept real-future inflation → budget relief. Accept negative Had-inversion into a present market result. Parallel if only / wish + could have for last month. Rebuild unless with subject + finite verb.

**D) I'll come cycling with you on Sunday provided the weather will hold.**

Provided the weather will hold wrongly inserts will into the condition. Same rule as if / as long as: no will in the proviso clause. Keep will come in the main clause and strip will from the weather proviso.

**Trap:** provided the weather will hold doubles future will and breaks the connector pattern.

Will inside the provided clause doubles future marking, so will hold is false — "I’ll come cycling with you on Sunday provided the weather is true."
**E) No sooner had we sat down than the fire alarm would go off.**

No sooner… than needs a simple past result (went off), not conditional would go off. No sooner is past sequencing, not a conditional frame. Leave would out of this narrative pattern.

**Trap:** would go off sneaks conditional mood into a past-sequencing idiom that wants went off.

No sooner… than sequences past events, so would go off doesn’t belong: "No sooner had we sat down than the fire alarm went off."

Accept booked / bring / holds as clean backshift, imperative, and proviso patterns. Reject will after provided. Do not force would onto a no sooner narrative.
